# Data-driven loyalty plan for Lee’s Market

**To:** David Lee, Marketing Manager  
**As of:** 27 August 2025

## Recommendation

Use Lee’s loyalty program to make shopping more relevant and convenient across stores, online shopping, and delivery. Start with a 90-day plan: first validate consented identity links and measurement definitions, then run an eight-week controlled pilot of relevant offers and useful meal or replenishment content. Keep the existing rewards rules during the test so Lee can isolate the effect of personalization before considering a broader points, tier, or gamification redesign.

Build offers around Lee’s product mix—fresh produce, meat and seafood, bakery and prepared foods, pantry, and household items. Test complementary meal baskets, discovery offers for products a member has not tried, and replenishment reminders based on observed purchase timing. These are hypotheses to test, not proven lifts. Include easy-to-redeem in-store offers for eligible shoppers who do not use digital channels, alongside opted-in email, SMS, app, or web messages.

## What Lee’s evidence says

The loyalty workbook reports 350,000 enrolled and 87,500 active members at 31 March 2024. Its reported engagement rate is 25% at each of nine listed dates from December 2021 through March 2024. Total membership and active-member counts each rose 75% between the first and last listed dates while the rate stayed flat. The workbook does not define “active” or “engagement.” [I1]

The retention workbook reports 62% retention in Q2 2024 against a 65% goal, up from 52% in Q4 2022. The cohort and denominator are unspecified, and its count of 1,000 is not reconciled to the loyalty-member totals. Treat this as a directional trend, not evidence that loyalty activity caused retention to improve. [I2]

Internal CRM material reports a 35% Q2 2024 redemption rate for CRM-driven offers, but does not define its denominator. It also reports a 15% increase in email open rates without a baseline or measurement period; names five customer segments, including Cultural Enthusiasts (25%) and Health-Conscious Shoppers (18%); and says targeted campaigns had 12% higher engagement without defining the comparison. SMS survey response was reportedly 20% better than email, but absolute response rates are not given. These are starting signals to validate, not established campaign effects. [I3]

Other internal channel figures say 58% of customers engaged with both online and in-store promotions in Q3 2023, 2,500 new Gen Z members were engaged by Q2 2024, and digital ads, signage, and online banners contributed to acquisition. These figures do not show that customers’ online and in-store activity is joined to the same loyalty identity. An October 2023 email says online loyalty integration was still being explored with IT; completion is not documented. [I4][I6]

A separate Q3 2023 email reports loyalty redemptions at 18% of sales revenue, with a “5% annual increase.” It does not clarify relative growth versus percentage-point change. This sales-revenue share is not the same measure as the 35% offer redemption rate. Keep the metrics separate until their definitions are reconciled. [I5]

External evidence supports testing relevant offers and in-store reach, but does not prove lift for Lee’s. BCG reported declining US engagement and loyalty compared with earlier research, although the accessible summary omits details needed to use those figures as a benchmark. PYMNTS reported that Kroger was testing personalized coupons for in-store-only shoppers; no result was reported. [E1][E2]

## 90-day test-and-learn plan

**Weeks 1–3: validate data and permissions.** Map available loyalty, POS, e-commerce, delivery, CRM, offer, and survey fields. Confirm whether a consented member ID can join store and digital transactions; measure match rates and document unmatched orders. Do not assume the join exists. Define active member, engagement, redemption denominator, and retention cohort/window. Record offer eligibility and assignment, exposure/delivery, activation, redemption, transaction lines, net sales, discounts, margin, channel/store, returns, and opt-outs. Review consent, permitted uses, retention, access, and opt-out controls for customers in the US and Canada before linking or activating data; the material reviewed does not document these controls.

Form test audiences from observable purchase behavior such as recency, frequency, category mix, channel, and declared preferences. Validate how existing segments are defined before using them. Do not infer ethnicity or sensitive traits from names or purchases. Confirm product availability with merchandising and store teams before sending offers.

**Weeks 4–11: run a randomized pilot.** Among eligible members, compare (A) a behavior-relevant offer or meal/replenishment message, (B) a generic offer with similar expected cost, and (C) business as usual. Randomize within lifecycle segment and store/channel where feasible; choose sample size using a power calculation. Include store-redeemable offers for eligible in-store-only shoppers and consented digital delivery. Keep reward value and terms clear and easy to use. Use a holdout so purchases that would have happened anyway are not counted as campaign impact.

**Week 12: decide what to scale.** Use incremental contribution margin per assigned eligible member versus business as usual as the primary outcome, after discounts and offer costs. Track engagement separately: define active as at least one identified purchase in a fixed period, then report active-member rate, repeat trips, category breadth, offer activation and redemption with explicit denominators, and cross-channel identity match rate. Compare retention for a fixed cohort and window. Monitor margin erosion, offer cannibalization, stockouts, opt-outs, and complaints. Treat opens and clicks as diagnostics, not success by themselves. Scale only treatments that improve incremental value while preserving customer experience; otherwise refine and retest.

## Evidence limits

Lee’s historical loyalty metrics have incomplete definitions, available records do not establish cross-channel identity linkage, and the public competitor example has no reported outcome. Do not promise a sales or retention lift in advance. Use the pilot to build a reliable baseline and test whether personalization, easier in-store redemption, or digital-to-store linkage creates incremental engagement and value.
